15570: "Suspended" describes something held in a middle state — not resting, not gone, but kept in between. This shows up in two main ways: physically (something hanging or floating) and figuratively (something temporarily stopped).

Something is suspended when it is held up in the air — either hanging down from something above it, or floating within a liquid or gas without sinking.

Examples:

  • A chandelier is suspended from the ceiling — it hangs down from above, not resting on any surface below.
  • Dust particles suspended in the air are floating within it, neither falling to the floor nor rising up.
  • Sediment suspended in water means tiny solid particles are drifting throughout the water — not dissolved, not settled at the bottom yet.

The essential image here: the thing is held in a between position — above a surface, below a support, or floating inside a medium.
Meaning 2: Temporarily Stopped or Put on Hold

When something that was active — a right, a rule, a process, an activity — is paused for a period of time but not permanently ended, we call it suspended. This is the figurative meaning, and it is very widely used.

The most important thing to understand about this meaning: suspended ≠ cancelled or finished. The thing still exists. It has just been put on pause. It could come back.

Examples:

  • A suspended driving licence — you are not allowed to drive for now, but once the suspension period ends or you meet certain conditions, you may get the licence back. It has not been taken away forever.
  • A suspended employee — the person has been told to stay away from work for a while, often while an investigation takes place. They have not been fired. Their employment is on hold.
  • Suspended negotiations — the talks between two parties have stopped for now, but neither side has walked away permanently. They may resume.
  • Suspended service — a train line, an internet subscription, or a utility has been temporarily halted.

Suspended sentence (legal)
A judge finds someone guilty of a crime but decides not to send them to prison right away. The prison sentence is real and official, but its execution is held over the person's head like a warning. As long as the person behaves — doesn't commit another crime, follows certain conditions — they may never serve that sentence. But if they break the terms, the suspended sentence is activated and they go to prison immediately. It is a sentence waiting to be carried out.

Suspended animation
A condition in which all the living processes of a body — breathing, heartbeat, metabolism — are slowed down to an almost undetectable level. The organism is not dead, but not fully alive in the normal sense either. Life itself is paused. You see this concept in science fiction (astronauts put to sleep in pods for century-long space journeys) and it also exists in nature — certain tiny organisms like tardigrades can survive extreme conditions by entering something very close to this state.

Suspended ceiling (also called a drop ceiling)
A second, lower ceiling installed below a building's actual structural ceiling. Panels or tiles hang from a metal grid that is itself suspended from the real ceiling above. This is common in offices and commercial buildings — it hides wiring, pipes, and ducts while creating a cleaner-looking ceiling.

Suspended in a liquid or gas (science)
In chemistry and physics, when tiny solid particles are distributed throughout a liquid or gas without dissolving into it, those particles are described as suspended. The mixture is called a suspension. Muddy water is a suspension — clay particles are suspended in the water. If you leave it undisturbed long enough, the particles eventually settle to the bottom. This is different from a solution (like salt water), where the substance fully dissolves and becomes invisible at the molecular level.
The Single Thread Running Through All Meanings

Whether physical or figurative, "suspended" always places something in a state of in-between:

  • Physically → between above and below — hanging, not resting on the ground
  • Figuratively → between active and ended — paused, not cancelled

This is why "suspended" often carries a feeling of things being unresolved or in limbo — things are hovering, waiting, not yet settled one way or the other.

Suspended vs. cancelled:
"Cancelled" means permanently ended. "Suspended" means temporarily stopped. A suspended flight could resume; a cancelled flight will not (that specific one is gone). A suspended law still exists on the books — a repealed law does not.

Suspended vs. terminated:
If a worker is terminated, they are fired — permanently. If they are suspended, they are only barred for a time. The employment relationship has not been fully cut.

Suspended vs. paused:
"Paused" is the everyday, informal way to say something similar. "Suspended" is more formal and often carries official weight — a suspension is usually a deliberate, formal decision by an authority (a court, a company, a government). You pause a video; you suspend a licence.

Suspended vs. resting:
A ball resting on a table is supported from below. A lamp that is suspended is supported from above and hangs. The direction of support matters for the physical meaning.

SenseWhat it meansExample

If something is suspended physically, it is hanging from above or floating within a medium, held in a position that is not resting on a surface below.

If something is suspended figuratively, it has been officially paused — stopped for a time, but not permanently ended. It could come back. The situation is unresolved, held in a kind of waiting state.

The word always implies something is caught between two states — and that is what makes it powerful and precise.
15571:
Suspense is the tense, anxious feeling of not knowing what is going to happen — while caring deeply about the outcome. It is the experience of waiting for an unknown result when something important is on the line.

Suspense is a feeling, not a thing you can see or touch. It lives inside you — in your mind and your body — whenever you are caught between not knowing and desperately wanting to know.
The Two Ingredients That Create Suspense

Every experience of suspense depends on two things working together.

The first is uncertainty. You must not know what will happen next. The moment you know the outcome, suspense disappears. This is why a thriller film grips you the first time you watch it, but never quite the same way again — once you know the ending, the uncertainty is gone.

The second is stakes. Something must matter to you. If a character is in danger, you only feel suspense if you care about that character. If you are waiting for exam results, you feel suspense because the result will affect your life. Without something important riding on the outcome, uncertainty alone only creates mild curiosity — not true suspense.

Remove either ingredient, and suspense evaporates. This is the simple formula: uncertainty + stakes = suspense.

Suspense sits in a unique emotional space. It is not exactly fear, and not exactly excitement, but it borrows from both. When you are in suspense, you feel a tightness — an inability to fully relax. You feel an urgent pull to find out what happens. You are aware that things could go wrong, or wonderfully right. Time feels slow because waiting feels endless.

People often describe suspense as being "on the edge of your seat" or "holding your breath." These expressions capture it well — your body actually responds to suspense. Your heart beats a little faster. You lean forward. You are physically caught in the uncertainty.

This is where you will encounter the word most frequently. Writers, directors, and storytellers deliberately craft suspense to keep audiences engaged. A story with no suspense feels flat and forgettable — there is no reason to keep watching or turning pages.

Suspense in stories is built in several classic ways. A character faces serious danger, and you don't know if they will survive. A detective must solve a mystery before the killer strikes again. Two people might confess their love for each other — or might not. These open questions create suspense because the outcome matters and you cannot predict it.

Sometimes, suspense is created through what's called dramatic irony — when the audience knows something the characters don't. Imagine a horror film where you can see a killer hiding in a dark closet, but the character walking through the house has no idea. You are desperate for the character to find out what you already know. This is a particularly powerful form of suspense, because your superior knowledge makes you feel both privileged and helpless.

Suspense also intensifies under time pressure. When a character has only minutes to defuse a bomb or catch a flight or stop a wedding, every ticking second adds weight to the uncertainty. The closer the deadline, the tighter the suspense.

Suspense is not limited to stories — it is a real emotion that surfaces regularly in everyday life. Any time you are waiting for an important outcome you cannot predict, you are experiencing suspense.

Waiting for the results of a medical test, hearing back after a job interview, watching a sports match where the score is tied in the final minutes, waiting backstage before stepping in front of an audience — all of these produce genuine suspense, because in each case, something important hangs on an unknown outcome.

Suspense is not always dark or frightening. It exists across a wide emotional range depending on what is at stake and whether you are hoping for something or fearing something.

In horror or thriller stories, suspense carries a fearful quality — you dread what might happen. In a romance, suspense feels hopeful — you're desperate for two people to find their way to each other. In sports, suspense feels electric and exciting. In a mystery, it feels like a burning curiosity — you need to know who did it.

In every case, the underlying experience is the same: uncertainty combined with stakes. But the emotional flavor shifts dramatically based on context.
How Suspense Differs From Similar Words

Understanding what suspense is not will sharpen your grasp of what it is.

Suspense vs. Anxiety — Anxiety is a general state of worry or nervousness, often without a clear focus. Suspense is specific — it is tied to a particular unknown outcome that is coming. You can feel anxious with no definite "moment of truth" on the horizon. But suspense always has a moment of truth approaching. You are always waiting for the reveal.

Suspense vs. Tension — Tension is a broader word for emotional strain or conflict, and it can exist between people, between opposing ideas, or in a difficult situation. Suspense is a particular type of tension — the kind that comes specifically from not knowing how something will turn out.

Suspense vs. Surprise — A surprise is the moment the unknown finally becomes known — the reveal itself. Suspense is everything that builds before the reveal. Suspense is the waiting; surprise is the arrival. The shocking twist at the end of a film is a surprise. The two hours of not knowing that made you desperate for the ending — that was the suspense.

Suspense vs. Fear — Fear is your reaction to something dangerous or threatening that is happening right now. Suspense is the fear (or hope) about something that hasn't happened yet. You feel fear when the monster appears. You feel suspense when you hear footsteps in the dark and don't yet know what is coming.
How the Word Is Used in English

Here are natural, common ways "suspense" appears:

"The film was full of suspense." — The movie constantly created that feeling of tense uncertainty.

"She kept us in suspense for hours before announcing the winner." — She made everyone wait and wonder, deliberately withholding the answer.

"The suspense was unbearable — I couldn't stop turning the pages." — The feeling was so intense it was almost painful.

"The suspense built slowly throughout the first half of the novel." — The feeling grew gradually over time.

"He announced the results slowly, clearly enjoying the suspense he was creating." — He took pleasure in the state of uncertainty he was producing in others.

You will also hear it used in compound phrases like "suspense novel," "suspense thriller," and "a scene of pure suspense."

Perhaps the most fascinating quality of suspense is that it can be deeply uncomfortable while also being strangely enjoyable. People actively seek it out — they pay to watch horror films, read thrillers late into the night, and follow nail-biting sports matches — precisely because they enjoy the feeling of not knowing. The discomfort of suspense is, paradoxically, part of its appeal. When the uncertainty is finally resolved, the relief or shock is all the more powerful for having been built up.

This is why skilled storytellers treat suspense as one of their most valuable tools. It is the engine that keeps people watching, reading, and caring about what comes next. It is, in the simplest terms, what makes you unable to look away.
15572:
Suspension means the act of hanging, holding up, or temporarily stopping something — either physically in space, or in time (pausing an activity or privilege).

Think of it this way: when something is "suspended," it isn't moving forward, it isn't resting on the ground, and it isn't finished. It is held — either literally dangling, or figuratively frozen mid-action.

The word covers several distinct real-world situations. Each one is a different flavour of that same core idea.
Meaning 1: Temporarily stopping or pausing something

This is the most common, everyday meaning.

Suspension = the temporary stopping of something that was ongoing, with the understanding that it may resume.

The government announced the suspension of peace talks.
The match was delayed due to the suspension of play because of rain.
The company issued a suspension of all hiring until further notice.

The key detail is temporary. A suspension is not a cancellation, an abolition, or a permanent end. It is a pause — a "hold" button pressed on something. The implication is always that the thing could restart.

This is why you hear "suspension of services," "suspension of a law," "suspension of payments," and so on.
Meaning 2: Removing someone from their role or privilege for a period of time

This is a specific, very common use — especially in schools, workplaces, and sports.

Suspension = an official punishment or precautionary measure where a person is barred from their position, school, or activity for a fixed time.

The student received a three-day suspension for fighting.
The footballer was handed a four-match suspension for his tackle.
The employee was placed on suspension while the investigation was underway.

Here, the person still holds their position in principle — they haven't been expelled or fired permanently — but they are forbidden from exercising their role for a defined period. A suspended student is still enrolled. A suspended employee is still technically employed. That is what makes it a suspension rather than a termination.

It can also serve as a precaution (not just a punishment). Someone might be suspended while an investigation is ongoing, before any guilt is established.
Meaning 3: The physical state of hanging or being held up without full support

This is the more literal, physical meaning.

Suspension = the state in which something hangs or is supported from above, or floats within a medium, without resting on the ground.

The chandelier hung in suspension from the ceiling.
The bridge deck is kept in suspension by thick steel cables.

A suspension bridge is the perfect example here — it's a bridge where the road deck is hung (suspended) from large cables that arc overhead, anchored at both ends. The deck doesn't sit on pillars beneath it; instead, it hangs from above. That physical relationship is literally suspension.
Meaning 4: In science — a mixture of particles in a liquid (or gas)

In chemistry and science, suspension has a precise technical meaning.

A suspension = a mixture in which small, undissolved solid particles are scattered throughout a liquid (or gas), but are not dissolved into it.

Muddy water is a suspension of soil particles in water.
Calamine lotion is a suspension — that's why the bottle says "shake well before use."

This is different from a solution (like salt water), where the substance fully dissolves and you can't see the individual particles. In a suspension, the particles remain separate and visible — and given enough time, they tend to settle at the bottom. That's why many medicines and paints are suspensions that need shaking: the particles sink when left still.
Meaning 5: In vehicles — the suspension system

Vehicle suspension = the mechanical system of springs, shock absorbers, and linkages connecting a vehicle's wheels to its body, designed to absorb shocks and keep the ride smooth.

The car's suspension was damaged after hitting the pothole.
Good suspension makes a huge difference on rough roads.

Think about driving over a bump. Without suspension, every jolt from the road would be transferred directly to the passengers. The suspension system absorbs those forces — it cushions the ride. The wheels bounce and move, but the cabin stays relatively stable. The word "suspension" fits because the vehicle's body is effectively suspended — held up and isolated — from the roughness of the wheels and the road.
Meaning 6: In music — a suspended note

In music theory, a suspension is a specific technique.

Musical suspension = when a note from one chord is held over (sustained) into the next chord, where it creates a temporary tension, before resolving to the expected note.

The composer used a suspension to build tension just before the final resolution.

Imagine a chord changes, but one note stubbornly lingers from the old chord for a beat — it clashes slightly with the new chord, creating a feeling of unresolved tension. That hanging, unresolved note is the suspension. It then "resolves" by moving to the note it was always meant to land on, and the tension releases. It's one of the most powerful tools in creating emotional pull in music.

This is a phrase you'll encounter often in discussions of literature, film, and storytelling.

Suspension of disbelief = the willingness of an audience to temporarily accept things in a story that they know are not real or logically impossible, in order to enjoy the fictional experience.

Watching a superhero movie requires a suspension of disbelief.
The novel was so well-written that readers maintained their suspension of disbelief throughout.

When you watch a film where a person flies, you know that's impossible. But you choose, temporarily, to set aside your scepticism — to "suspend" your disbelief — so that you can be fully absorbed by the story. If a film is poorly made, your suspension of disbelief "breaks" and you're suddenly aware again that you're watching something fake.

The phrase was coined by the poet Samuel Taylor Coleridge, and it has become an essential concept in how we talk about storytelling and audience engagement.
A Quick Map of All the Meanings

Suspension as pausing time → stopping an activity, service, or law temporarily.

Suspension as removing a person → barring someone from their role for a fixed period as punishment or precaution.

Suspension as hanging in space → something physically held up or dangling (suspension bridge).

Suspension as a mixture → solid particles dispersed in a liquid without dissolving (muddy water, calamine).

Suspension as a vehicle system → the mechanism that absorbs road shocks and smooths the ride.

Suspension in music → a held note that creates tension before resolving.

Suspension of disbelief → choosing to accept fiction as real, temporarily, to enjoy a story.

In every case, something is held in an in-between state:

  • A paused activity is between running and ended.
  • A suspended person is between active and dismissed.
  • A hanging object is between flying freely and resting on the ground.
  • A particle in a suspension is between dissolved and settled.
  • A vehicle's body is between the roughness of the road and a smooth cabin.
  • A suspended musical note is between one chord and its resolution.
  • A suspended belief is between full acceptance and full scepticism.

That in-between, held, neither-here-nor-there quality is the soul of the word "suspension."
15573:
Suspicion is a feeling or belief that something wrong, bad, or dishonest is happening — or has happened — even though you don't have solid proof of it. It sits in the mental space between "I don't know" and "I'm sure." You feel that something is probably true, but you can't confirm it yet.

Think of it this way: if you come home and notice your cookie jar is empty, and your little brother has chocolate crumbs on his shirt, you have a suspicion that he ate the cookies. You didn't see him do it. You have no confession. But something in your mind says, "It was probably him." That mental state — that uneasy feeling of "I think something is going on" — is suspicion.

This word carries three closely related but distinct meanings, and fluency means understanding all three.

1. A feeling that someone has done something wrong

This is the most common use. Suspicion here is an internal feeling — a hunch, a doubt, a quiet alarm bell going off in your mind — that a person has behaved dishonestly, illegally, or wrongfully. It is not an accusation. It is not a fact. It is a belief that hasn't been proven.

She had a suspicion that her business partner was hiding money.
His suspicious behavior raised suspicion among his coworkers.

Notice that suspicion here is something you experience about another person. You are the one doing the suspecting.

2. The state of being suspected by others

This is the flip side. Here, suspicion is something that falls on a person — it describes the condition of being thought guilty or dishonest by others. You are not doing the suspecting; you are the one being suspected.

After the money went missing, everyone in the office fell under suspicion.
The detective said that no one in the family was above suspicion.

When someone is "under suspicion," it means other people think they may have done something wrong. It doesn't mean they actually did it — just that others are watching them and doubting them.

3. A very slight trace or hint of something (figurative)

This third meaning is softer and has nothing to do with wrongdoing. It's used to describe a very, very small amount of something — so little that you almost can't detect it, but it's just barely there.

The soup had just a suspicion of lemon in it.
There was a suspicion of a smile on her lips.

This usage treats "suspicion" almost like the word "hint" or "trace." It paints a picture of something so faint it might just be your imagination — but it's there.
What Makes Suspicion Different from Similar Ideas

Suspicion is not proof. This is the single most important thing to understand. A person can be completely innocent and still be under suspicion. Suspicion is a mental state, not a fact. Courts of law, for example, treat suspicion and guilt as entirely separate things.

Suspicion is not accusation. An accusation is when you openly state, out loud or formally, that you believe someone did something wrong. Suspicion can live quietly inside your mind without ever being spoken. You can suspect someone your whole life and never say a word about it.

Suspicion is not certainty. If you know someone did something wrong, you don't just suspect them — you have evidence, a confession, or witnessed it yourself. Suspicion always carries a degree of doubt. The moment doubt disappears and you have proof, the suspicion transforms into something stronger — knowledge or conviction.

Suspicion is not paranoia, but it can tip into it. Healthy suspicion is a reasonable response to something that seems off. Paranoia is excessive, irrational suspicion that has no real basis. The word "suspicion" itself is neutral — it doesn't tell you whether the feeling is well-founded or not.
The Emotional Weight of the Word

Suspicion is rarely a comfortable feeling. To experience suspicion is to feel uneasy, to sense that something is not right, to be alert but uncertain. It often involves a kind of inner tension — you want to trust, but something is stopping you.

On the receiving end — being suspected — is equally uncomfortable. It feels unfair if you're innocent, and it can damage relationships and reputations even without proof of any wrongdoing. This is why the phrase "innocent until proven guilty" matters so much in legal settings: suspicion alone should never be treated as truth.

Learning a word fully means knowing how it lives inside phrases and expressions. Here are the most important ones:

Under suspicion — being suspected of wrongdoing by others. "Three employees are under suspicion."

Above suspicion — so trusted or beyond reproach that no one would dream of suspecting them. "She had worked there for 40 years and was considered above suspicion."

On suspicion of — suspected of committing a specific act, often used in legal or police contexts. "He was arrested on suspicion of fraud."

To arouse / raise suspicion — to cause others to start suspecting something. "Her sudden wealth raised suspicion."

To cast suspicion on someone — to make it seem as though a particular person might be guilty. "The misleading evidence cast suspicion on the wrong man."

To fall under suspicion — to begin to be suspected. "After the theft, everyone in the building fell under suspicion."

With suspicion — in a distrustful or doubtful way. "She looked at him with suspicion."
A Quick Way to Remember It

Whenever you encounter the word suspicion, ask yourself one question: "Who is doubting whom — and about what?"

It will almost always be one of the three cases above: someone feeling doubt about another person's honesty; someone being doubted by others; or a very faint trace of something barely present.

That triangle — the doubter, the doubted, and the unproven wrongdoing between them — is the soul of the word.
15574:
"Suspicious" is about doubt and distrust — a feeling that something is wrong, dishonest, or dangerous, even without solid proof.

But here is the most important thing to understand about this word: it works in two directions, and knowing both is the key to mastering it.

Meaning 1 — A Person Who Feels Doubt or Distrust

When "suspicious" describes a person, it means that person has an uneasy feeling that something is not right. They sense that someone might be lying, hiding something, or behaving in a bad way — even if they can't fully prove it yet.

Think of it as a gut feeling of "I don't think I can trust this."

Examples:

  • She was suspicious of his sudden kindness. → She didn't trust it. Something felt off to her.
  • The detective became suspicious when the witness changed his story. → The change made the detective feel that the witness was hiding something.
  • I was suspicious of the deal — it seemed too good to be true. → The person doubted whether the deal was honest.

In this meaning, you will almost always see the structure: suspicious of someone or something.

Meaning 2 — A Thing, Person, or Situation That Causes Suspicion in Others

When "suspicious" describes a thing, a behavior, or a situation, it means that thing has qualities that make people feel uneasy or distrustful. It looks wrong, strange, or potentially dishonest — it raises red flags in people's minds.

Think of it as something sending the signal: "Look at me carefully — something might not be right here."

Examples:

  • Police found a suspicious package near the station. → The package looked or seemed dangerous or strange — it made people feel something was wrong.
  • He was behaving in a suspicious manner. → His behavior was odd in a way that made others doubt or distrust him.
  • There were suspicious circumstances surrounding her disappearance. → The circumstances didn't seem normal and made people feel something bad or dishonest had happened.
The Relationship Between the Two Meanings

These two meanings are really two sides of the same coin:

  • Meaning 2 causes Meaning 1.
  • A suspicious thing (Meaning 2) makes a person feel suspicious (Meaning 1).

For example: The man's suspicious behavior (Meaning 2) made the shopkeeper suspicious of him (Meaning 1).

Once you see this connection, using the word correctly becomes very natural.

"Suspicious" carries a feeling of quiet alertness mixed with unease. It is not quite fear, and it is not quite certainty of wrongdoing. It lives in the space between feeling something is wrong and actually knowing it is wrong.

This is why you can say "I was suspicious, but I had no proof." Suspicion is a feeling, not a confirmed fact.

You can be a little suspicious or very suspicious. The word itself doesn't fix the degree, but you can adjust it:

  • slightly suspicious → a small, quiet doubt
  • deeply/highly suspicious → a strong, intense feeling of distrust
  • immediately suspicious → the distrust came fast

These are the most natural ways "suspicious" is used. Learning these combinations will help you use the word fluently:

With people (Meaning 1):

  • be suspicious of someone/something
  • grow/become suspicious
  • arouse someone's suspicion (make someone feel suspicious)
  • rightly/understandably suspicious (their suspicion was justified)

With things/behavior (Meaning 2):

  • suspicious behavior / activity / circumstances
  • a suspicious person / vehicle / package
  • suspicious-looking (something that appears suspicious)
  • nothing suspicious ("Police found nothing suspicious." = no signs of wrongdoing)
Connotation — Is It Positive or Negative?

In most situations, "suspicious" carries a negative or cautionary connotation. It suggests something is potentially bad, dishonest, or dangerous.

However, being suspicious of something is not always painted as a flaw. Sometimes it is wise to be suspicious — especially if you are right to be. In that case, the word is neutral-to-positive:

  • She was rightly suspicious of the company's promises. → Her suspicion was sensible and justified.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Understanding how "suspicious" differs from close words will sharpen your grasp of it:

Doubtful → about uncertainty. You're not sure if something is true. It is softer and doesn't always carry distrust. "I'm doubtful he'll arrive on time" is about uncertainty, not dishonesty.

Distrustful → like Meaning 1 of suspicious, but stronger and more settled. If you are distrustful, it is often a general attitude. If you are suspicious, it is usually triggered by a specific person or event.

Wary → careful and cautious, often from past experience. It doesn't necessarily mean you think something dishonest is happening — just that you are being careful. "I'm wary of dogs" doesn't mean you think dogs are dishonest.

Shady (informal) → very similar to Meaning 2 of suspicious, but more informal and stronger. "That deal sounds shady" strongly implies dishonesty.

Questionable → similar to Meaning 2, but gentler and more polite. It suggests doubt without strongly implying wrongdoing.

What it meansExample
PersonFeels doubt or distrustShe was suspicious of him.
Thing/BehaviorLooks or seems wrong, causes distrustSuspicious behavior was reported.

The single most important thing to remember: "suspicious" always lives in the zone of doubt, not certainty. It is the feeling that something might be wrong — and that feeling can belong to a person, or it can come from a thing.
15575:
"Sustain" means to keep something going, alive, or strong — to stop it from fading, failing, or collapsing. It is an act of continuous support. You don't just help something once; you keep supporting it so it can continue to exist or function.

That is the core idea. But "sustain" is a rich word with several closely related meanings, all connected by that same thread of keeping something up. Here is every one of them, explained clearly.

Meaning 1: To keep something going over time

This is the most common everyday use. When you sustain something, you ensure it doesn't stop, slow down, or disappear.

She sustained her concentration for three straight hours during the exam. The couple found it difficult to sustain a conversation after years apart. The company struggled to sustain its early momentum. A singer can sustain a musical note — holding it long and steady without letting it waver or drop.

In every case, something is already happening, and "sustain" is the force that keeps it alive and moving forward.

Meaning 2: To provide what something needs to survive

Here, "sustain" means to nourish, fuel, or support the very existence of something — to be its lifeline.

Water and sunlight sustain plants. The village was sustained by fishing for generations. Hope sustained him through the darkest years of his imprisonment.

In this sense, to sustain something is to be the source without which it would wither and die. Remove the sustaining force, and the thing collapses.

Meaning 3: To hold up weight or physical pressure

"Sustain" can also mean to bear or carry a load without breaking or giving way.

The old bridge could no longer sustain the weight of heavy vehicles. The building's foundation is engineered to sustain enormous downward pressure.

Think of this as "hold up." The structure receives the weight and keeps standing under it.

Meaning 4: To suffer or experience something negative

This is crucial, and it is the meaning that trips up most learners, because it feels opposite to all the others. When someone sustains an injury, damage, or a loss, it means they experience or suffer it — they receive it and carry it.

The athlete sustained a serious knee injury during the final. The coastal town sustained heavy damage from the hurricane. The firm sustained significant financial losses in the first quarter.

Notice: "sustain" here does not mean the person supported the injury or wanted it. It simply means it happened to them and they are now bearing it. Whenever you see sustain + something bad, read it as suffer or experience.

Meaning 5: To uphold, confirm, or back something up

"Sustain" can mean to support the truth or validity of a claim, argument, or theory — to act as evidence that something is correct.

The forensic evidence sustained his claim that he was innocent. Her decade of research sustains the theory that chronic stress accelerates aging.

This is especially prominent in courtrooms. When a lawyer objects to a question and the judge says "Objection sustained," it means the judge agrees — the objection is valid and upheld. The question is stopped. The opposite ruling is "Overruled," meaning the judge disagrees and the question stands.

Meaning 6: To endure hardship without breaking

Finally, "sustain" can describe surviving something relentlessly difficult — going through it and coming out the other side without collapsing.

The team sustained months of harsh public criticism without losing their confidence. She sustained enormous emotional pressure and emerged even stronger.

Here, sustaining is an act of resilience — you are being battered by something, and you are not breaking.
The one thread that ties everything together

No matter which meaning you encounter, ask yourself: Is something being kept going, kept alive, or kept standing?

Whether it's a conversation, a life, a building, a legal objection, or an argument — "sustain" is always about continuation, support, and endurance. Even the "suffer an injury" meaning fits this pattern: the injury is received into the body and carried forward in time. Something is being borne and held.
How to recognize each meaning at a glance

When you see "sustain" followed by effort, a conversation, growth, a pace, or attention — it means keep it going.

When it's followed by a person, life, a crop, or hope — it means provide what's needed to survive.

When it's followed by weight, a load, or pressure — it means hold it up physically.

When it's followed by an injury, damage, a loss, or a defeat — it means suffer or experience it.

When it's followed by a claim, a theory, or an argument — it means support or confirm it.

When it's followed by criticism, hardship, or adversity — it means endure it without giving in.

Master these six patterns and you will recognize "sustain" correctly in every sentence you ever encounter it in — in literature, journalism, law, science, or everyday speech.
15576:
Sustainability means the ability to keep something going for a long time — without using it up, breaking it down, or causing harm that cannot be repaired.

Think of it this way: if you have a fruit tree, and you pick only as many fruits as the tree can grow back each season, the tree keeps producing fruit — for you, your children, and their children. That is sustainable. But if you chop the tree down for all its fruit at once, it is gone forever. That is unsustainable.

So sustainability is about finding the balance between using what we have and preserving it for the future.

The most widely accepted definition of sustainability comes from a 1987 United Nations report. It says sustainability means meeting the needs of people today without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

This one sentence contains two important ideas:

  1. Present needs matter. People alive today have real and legitimate needs — food, energy, jobs, shelter. Sustainability is not about denying those needs.
  2. Future needs matter equally. The way we meet our needs today must not destroy the resources, systems, and conditions that people in the future will depend on.

It is fundamentally a question of fairness across time.

Over time, thinkers and policymakers realized that sustainability is not just about nature and resources. It has three deeply connected dimensions, often called the "three pillars":

1. Environmental Sustainability

This is the most familiar pillar. It is about protecting the natural world — the air, water, soil, forests, oceans, and biodiversity — so that ecosystems continue to function and support life.

Examples: reducing carbon emissions to slow climate change, stopping overfishing so fish populations can recover, protecting rainforests so they continue producing oxygen and rainfall.

2. Economic Sustainability

This pillar is about building economies and businesses that can remain stable and productive over the long term — without depending on practices that will eventually collapse.

A business that makes money today by polluting a river may thrive short-term, but it destroys the water supply the community needs. That is economically unsustainable in the long run. True economic sustainability means creating wealth in ways that can continue indefinitely.

3. Social Sustainability

This pillar focuses on people — communities, cultures, health, justice, and equality. A society is socially sustainable when its people have access to fair treatment, good working conditions, education, and healthcare, and when communities can remain stable and function well over generations.

For example, if a factory pays workers so little that they remain in poverty, that creates long-term social instability and suffering — that is not socially sustainable.

Why All Three Are Linked

These pillars do not exist independently. Destroying the environment eventually destroys economies (no clean water = no farming). Economic inequality creates social instability. Social unrest leads to environmental neglect. Sustainability, fully understood, means managing all three together.

A key insight within sustainability is that everything is connected. Actions in one area ripple into others. Sustainability encourages us to look at the whole system — not just the immediate effect of an action, but its long-term and wide-reaching consequences.

For example, burning coal for cheap electricity seems purely economic, but it releases carbon dioxide, which warms the planet, which floods coastal cities, which displaces millions of people, which creates social and economic crises. Sustainability asks us to trace these connections before acting.

Understanding what the word does not mean helps sharpen what it does mean:

  • It is not about zero consumption. Sustainability does not mean using nothing. It means using wisely and within what can be replenished or maintained.
  • It is not just about the environment. As explained above, it equally includes economic and social dimensions.
  • It is not a fixed end-state. Sustainability is a continuous process of adjustment, not a destination you permanently arrive at.
  • It is not the same as "going green." "Going green" typically refers narrowly to environmental actions. Sustainability is a broader concept that includes whether those green actions are also economically viable and socially fair.
How the Word Is Used in Different Contexts

The word sustainability is used across many fields, and while the core meaning stays the same, the emphasis shifts:

  • In business: "We are committed to the sustainability of our operations" — meaning the company wants to operate profitably in the long term without depleting resources or harming communities.
  • In agriculture: "Sustainable farming" refers to growing food in ways that maintain soil health, water quality, and biodiversity over generations — rather than methods that boost short-term yield but exhaust the land.
  • In urban planning: Sustainability refers to designing cities that are livable, low-emission, resource-efficient, and socially inclusive for decades to come.
  • In finance: "Sustainability investing" (also called ESG investing) means choosing to invest in companies that score well on environmental, social, and governance factors — not just short-term profit.
  • In everyday conversation: Someone might say "I'm not sure this habit is sustainable" — meaning they cannot keep it up over time. This is a looser, more personal use of the word, but it captures the same essence: can this continue?
The Deeper Philosophical Weight of the Word

Sustainability carries a certain moral weight. It quietly asks a question: Are we being responsible stewards of the world we inherited?

It implies that we do not fully "own" the Earth or its resources in an absolute sense — we are, in a way, borrowing from the future. How we treat what we have borrowed reflects our values. This is why sustainability is not just a policy concept or business strategy — it is also an ethical position.

AspectWhat it means

Sustainability is the capacity to continue a process, system, or way of life over the long term — by ensuring that what we consume or use is not being permanently destroyed or depleted. It rests on three interconnected pillars: environmental (protecting nature), economic (building lasting prosperity), and social (ensuring human wellbeing and fairness). Its central moral principle is that the present generation should not steal from future generations. When something is sustainable, it can keep going indefinitely. When it is unsustainable, it eventually collapses or causes irreversible harm.
15577:
Sustainable means: able to continue for a long time without exhausting itself, causing lasting damage, or destroying the very conditions that allow it to keep going.

If something is sustainable, it can keep running indefinitely — it doesn't burn through what it needs, it doesn't create harm that builds up until it collapses, and it doesn't borrow from the future to pay for the present.

The opposite — unsustainable — means something that will eventually run out, break down, or cause so much damage that it can no longer continue.

Imagine a small village next to a forest. The villagers use wood from the forest to cook and heat their homes. If they cut down only as many trees as the forest can grow back each year, the wood supply never runs out. The village keeps going. That's sustainable.

But if they cut down trees faster than the forest can regrow, eventually there are no trees left. The village collapses. That's unsustainable.

This is the core logic: taking or doing only as much as can be replenished, recovered, or absorbed without permanent damage. The system stays in balance. It doesn't eat into its own future.

Experts often describe sustainability through three connected lenses:

Environmental — not damaging nature faster than it can heal or regenerate. Using resources at a rate the planet can keep up with.

Social — not causing harm to people or communities in ways that accumulate over time. Ensuring that people's health, dignity, and wellbeing aren't quietly being eroded.

Economic — not spending or depending on resources in a way that leads to eventual financial collapse. Keeping a system financially viable long-term.

A truly sustainable action ideally holds up well on all three. In everyday use, though, people often focus on just one — most commonly the environmental one.

In the environment and nature:

Sustainable farming uses methods that keep soil healthy year after year, so it can keep producing crops without destroying the land over time. Sustainable fishing means catching only as many fish as the population can replace through natural reproduction. Sustainable energy — like solar, wind, or hydropower — generates electricity without burning through finite resources like coal, oil, or gas, which will eventually run out.

In business and economics:

A sustainable business model can keep generating revenue without depending on something temporary or destructive. A company that profits by depleting a rare natural resource it can't replace isn't truly sustainable — it'll eventually run out of that resource and collapse. Sustainable growth means growing at a pace the organization can actually support: not so fast that it exhausts its employees, overstretches its finances, or sacrifices the quality that made it successful.

In personal life:

A sustainable workout routine is one you can genuinely keep up for months and years without injuring yourself or burning out. A sustainable diet is one that keeps you healthy over the long run — not so extreme or miserable that you'll eventually abandon it. A sustainable pace at work means you're not operating at a level that will inevitably lead to exhaustion or breakdown.

In international policy and development:

Sustainable development is one of the most important phrases in modern global policy. Its classic definition — from a landmark 1987 United Nations report called the Brundtland Report — is: development that meets the needs of people today without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. This became the foundation of how governments and international organizations think about economic growth, poverty, and the environment. The United Nations' 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), adopted in 2015, are built entirely around this idea.

Sustainability isn't a simple yes-or-no quality. Something can be more or less sustainable on a spectrum.

  • Recycling paper is more sustainable than throwing it away, but making paper from responsibly managed forests is even more sustainable.
  • A twelve-hour workday might be unsustainable over years, but a nine-hour day might be manageable for some people over the long term.
  • Using a little less water is more sustainable than wasting it, but redesigning agriculture to need far less water is even more so.

The word also carries an implied long time horizon. Something that seems to work fine for ten years but causes catastrophe in fifty is not truly sustainable — it just hasn't failed yet. Sustainability asks: will this still be working, and working well, in twenty, fifty, or a hundred years?
The Word Is About Time, Balance, and Consequence

These three ideas are what "sustainable" is really built on:

  • Time: Can this keep going? Not just today, but long into the future?
  • Balance: Is it in harmony with what it depends on — soil, money, energy, human effort, trust?
  • Consequence: Are there hidden costs building up quietly that will eventually force a stop?

If a practice, system, business, or habit answers all three well, it earns the label sustainable.
A Common Trap: Vagueness and Overuse

"Sustainable" has become one of the most used — and misused — words in modern business and marketing. Companies sometimes stick the label on products to seem responsible without it meaning much in practice. This is called greenwashing: using the vocabulary of sustainability without the substance. A product might be called "sustainable" because it uses slightly less plastic, even if its manufacturing still causes serious environmental harm.

When you encounter the word in advertising or branding, it's always worth asking: sustainable in what way, over what time period, and compared to what? A precise and honest use of the word should be able to answer those questions clearly.

"Sustainable" appears very frequently with certain words. Getting familiar with these will help you recognize and use the word naturally:

  • sustainable development
  • sustainable growth
  • sustainable energy / sustainable power
  • sustainable farming / sustainable agriculture
  • sustainable lifestyle
  • sustainable future
  • sustainable business / sustainable business model
  • sustainable pace
  • environmentally sustainable
  • financially sustainable
  • socially sustainable
  • economically sustainable

• "The government pledged to transition to sustainable energy sources within the next two decades."
  • "Her eighty-hour work weeks weren't sustainable — she burned out within six months."
  • "The startup's early success depended on steep discounts that weren't part of a sustainable business model."
  • "Indigenous communities in the Amazon have practiced sustainable land management for centuries."
  • "He made small, sustainable changes to his diet rather than attempting an extreme overhaul he knew he'd quit."
  • "The peace agreement was fragile; lasting stability would require more sustainable political reforms."

Sustainable = able to continue over a long period without exhausting resources, causing irreversible damage, or undermining the conditions that allow it to keep going.

It is fundamentally a word about time, balance, and consequence. Something sustainable stays in a kind of harmony with what it depends on. It doesn't silently borrow from the future, doesn't quietly erode what it needs, and doesn't carry hidden costs that will eventually force it to stop. It is built to last — and to keep working — without leaving wreckage behind.
15578:
Something is sustained when it:

  1. Continues for a long period of time,
  2. Doesn't stop, restart repeatedly, or fade away, and
  3. Keeps its strength or intensity throughout.

All three of those ideas live inside the word at once. That's what makes it precise. It's not just "this lasted a while." It's "this lasted, kept going, and held its level."

Imagine a singer holding a long note. If they sing it and it immediately fades, that's not sustained. But if they hold it out — steady, strong, and full — for many seconds without wavering, that is a sustained note.

Or imagine a fire. A single spark isn't sustained. A fire that burns powerfully for hours without dying down — that is.

The word gives you the picture of something that endures without weakening.

To sharpen the meaning, here's what sustained things are not:

  • Brief or momentary — a sustained thing is the opposite of a flash
  • Sporadic — sporadic means on-and-off; sustained means consistently going
  • Intermittent — stopping and starting with gaps in between
  • Fleeting — here and quickly gone
  • Fading — sustained things don't lose their intensity; they hold it
How It Differs From Similar Words

This is where many learners get confused. These words seem close, but they're not the same.

Sustained vs. Prolonged
"Prolonged" only tells you that something lasted longer than usual. It says nothing about whether it stayed strong or consistent. Something prolonged might have been weak, uneven, or gradually fading — it just went on too long.

"Sustained" adds the idea that the quality or intensity was maintained throughout.

A prolonged meeting — a meeting that went on longer than expected.
A sustained campaign — a campaign that was actively kept up at full force over a long time.

Sustained vs. Continuous
"Continuous" is more absolute — it means without any interruption at all, not even a pause. "Sustained" is a bit more flexible. It means the thing was consistently maintained and didn't diminish, but it doesn't require that there was zero pause ever. The focus of "sustained" is on the maintenance of level, while the focus of "continuous" is on no break in time.

Sustained vs. Persistent
"Persistent" describes something or someone that keeps coming back or refuses to give up, often in the face of obstacles. It has a stubborn, recurring quality to it. "Sustained" is more about something that just keeps going steadily, without necessarily fighting opposition.

Persistent pain — pain that keeps returning, perhaps coming in waves.
Sustained pain — pain that stays elevated consistently without letting up.

Sustained vs. Steady
"Steady" means regular and even, without big fluctuations. It's about rhythm and stability. "Sustained" is about duration and maintenance of level. Something can be steady but brief. Something sustained is steady over a long stretch of time.

Effort and work:

"It took years of sustained effort to become a skilled writer."

The writer didn't just try hard for a week and stop. They kept putting in consistent, strong effort year after year.

"The athlete showed sustained performance throughout the entire season."

Their performance didn't start great and then crash — it stayed at a high level from beginning to end.

Focus and attention:

"The student demonstrated sustained concentration during the five-hour exam."

Her attention didn't waver or weaken halfway through. It held steady.

"The documentary failed to hold the audience's sustained interest."

Viewers were interested at first but couldn't maintain that interest all the way through.

Growth and economics:

"The country experienced sustained economic growth for two decades."

The economy didn't just have one good year. It kept growing, without collapsing, for a long and steady stretch.

Natural forces:

"The bridge was engineered to withstand sustained winds of 150 km/h."

Not a single powerful gust — but wind blowing at that speed continuously over a period of time.

"The patient suffered a sustained fever for four days."

The fever didn't come and go — it stayed elevated the whole time without breaking.

Combat and pressure:

"The city endured a sustained attack for three weeks."

Not a quick raid — a prolonged, relentless offensive that didn't stop.

"She faced sustained pressure from her employer to meet the deadline."

The pressure didn't ease up after a day. It kept coming, day after day.

Applause:

"The performance received sustained applause from the audience."

The clapping didn't quickly die down — it kept going vigorously for a long time, showing genuine appreciation.

Music:

"The vocalist held a sustained note for eight full seconds."

The note didn't fade or waver — it was held at full strength throughout.

A campaign or cause:

"It was only through sustained advocacy that the law was eventually changed."

One protest wasn't enough. It took continued, consistent, long-term advocacy to make the change happen.

In a courtroom, you'll sometimes hear a judge say: "Objection sustained."

Here, "sustained" means upheld or accepted as valid. The judge is agreeing with the lawyer's objection and ruling in their favor.

So a sustained objection is one the judge accepted — the question was not allowed to stand.

This is a specific, formal meaning used only in legal settings. It's quite different from the main meaning of "continuing over time," but it's worth knowing because you'll encounter it if you read legal writing, watch courtroom dramas, or study law.

Here's the most important thing to hold onto:

"Sustained" isn't just about how long something lasts — it's about how it lasts.

A short sprint and a marathon are both runs. But a marathon is sustained — it demands that you keep going without breaking down. The word carries a built-in sense of endurance combined with maintained quality. Something sustained doesn't just exist for a long time; it holds its ground over that entire time.

This is why the word feels strong and positive in contexts like "sustained effort" or "sustained growth." It implies not just duration, but the kind of steady, unbroken commitment that takes real strength to maintain.

Avoid using "sustained" for:

  • Things that are naturally instantaneous — a decision, a moment of realization, a single glance
  • Things that happen repeatedly but with gaps — say "repeated" or "intermittent" instead
  • Things that fade progressively — say "prolonged" if that's what you mean, or "gradual"
Sustained describes something that continues for a long time, keeps its strength or intensity throughout, and doesn't fade, stop, or become uneven along the way.
15579:
Sustenance means food and drink — the things a living being needs to stay alive, maintain energy, and function. It is what keeps the body going. When you eat a meal after a long, tiring day, that meal is your sustenance. When a traveler in the desert finds water, that water is their sustenance.

The word carries a tone of necessity. Sustenance is not a luxury or a treat — it is what a living thing fundamentally needs in order to survive. This is an important quality of the word. You would not use "sustenance" to describe a birthday cake eaten for fun. But you would use it to describe the bread and water that kept a prisoner alive.

Here is where the word becomes richer. Sustenance does not always refer to physical food. It is also used figuratively to describe anything that nourishes, supports, or keeps something going — whether that is a person's spirit, mind, heart, or even a system or cause.

For example, a lonely person living far from family might say that letters from home were their only sustenance. A passionate reader might say that books are the sustenance of their mind. A deeply religious person might say that prayer is the sustenance of their soul. In all these cases, the speaker means: "This is the thing that feeds me, supports me, and keeps me going — without it, I would wither."

This figurative use follows the same logic as the literal one. Just as the body needs food to survive, the mind, heart, and spirit need certain things to remain alive and well. Sustenance, in this sense, is whatever fulfills that deep need.
The third, more abstract meaning — the act of sustaining

Less commonly, sustenance can refer to the act or process of maintaining something — keeping it alive, keeping it going, or supporting its continued existence over time. In this use, the word shifts from being a thing (food) to being a concept (maintenance or support).

For example: "The sustenance of a healthy democracy requires an informed public." Here, sustenance means the ongoing effort of keeping something alive and functioning. Or: "The organization depended on donations for its sustenance." This means the organization depended on donations to keep existing.
The tone and register of the word

Sustenance is a formal and somewhat literary word. You are more likely to see it in writing — novels, essays, speeches, or serious conversations — than in everyday casual speech. A person would rarely say "I need some sustenance" in the way they would say "I need some food." When someone does use it in speech, it often adds a sense of gravity or importance to what they are saying.
How it compares to similar words

Food is the everyday, neutral word for things you eat. Nourishment is close to sustenance in meaning, but it puts the emphasis on the nutritional benefit — on what the food does to make you healthy and strong. Sustenance puts the emphasis on survival and maintenance — on the bare necessity of keeping something alive and going. It has a slightly more serious, urgent quality than either of those words.
A quick summary to lock it in

Sustenance means:
one — food and drink that keeps a living being alive (its most direct meaning); two — anything that feeds, supports, or nourishes a person's inner life (its figurative meaning); and three — the ongoing act or process of maintaining something (its most abstract meaning). In all three senses, the central idea is the same: sustenance is whatever is necessary to keep something — a body, a mind, a spirit, or a system — going.
